A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same marketplace, retaining the discovery framework, pricing formulation, and core experiments despite the changed title and organization. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original discovery experiments using NYC datasets and simulated pricing evaluations, including School/Taxi results, aggregate task performance, and in-sample/out-of-sample profit comparisons.

after.justification: V2 retains original discovery and pricing evaluations and adds buyer-prior learning simulations with convergence and sensitivity results in RQ3 and Appendix D.2.

M1.justification: V1 takes the buyer-type prior as given. V2 adds a Bayesian learning procedure using observed stopping times, posterior smoothing, and batched updates (Section 5, Algorithm 1, RQ3). It also revises the buyer stopping DP from tracking the highest performance metric to surplus-based choices.

E1.justification: The NYC corpus and classification/regression coverage remain. V2 adds the distinct task of recovering an unknown buyer-type distribution through simulated interactions, including random and differently skewed populations (RQ3 and Appendix D.2), extending coverage beyond discovery and pricing with a supplied prior.

E2.justification: Retained discovery comparisons use DATA-ALL, DATA-ALT, and AutoML. Pricing retains Independent, Shift, Jiggle, and the all-metrics optimal reference. The new Myerson attribution does not introduce another evaluated baseline; prior-learning plots compare settings of the proposed learner.

E3.justification: New prior-learning experiments evaluate KL divergence using five buyer types, ten metric states, and a 15-step horizon, varying learning rates, batch sizes of 10/100, and 1,000/10,000 learning rounds. These introduce a substantial evaluation protocol; the retained discovery and pricing settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds extensive sensitivity analyses of prior learning across learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, interaction budgets, and distribution skew (Figures 5–13). V1's qualitative School/Taxi inspection identifying useful neighborhood features is removed. The existing out-of-sample pricing robustness comparison remains.

E5.justification: The pricing evaluation retains its 100-problem setup and profit-distribution plots. New learning curves introduce no stated independent repeat counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Learning rounds and batch sizes describe the learning procedure rather than repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V2 adds KL-divergence trajectories showing convergence and learning-rate/batch-size effects, including noisier constant-rate learning and smoothing with larger batches. It removes v1's separate School/Taxi performance curves and feature-level findings. Aggregate discovery and pricing results are retained as Figures 3 and 4, without demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 adds stopping-likelihood derivations, an identifiability assumption, the Cost of Estimation Error definition, and Theorem 5.2 with new Appendix C derivations claiming bounded revenue loss under estimated priors and transitions. It also revises the stopping recurrence. The original MILP approximation and discovery guarantees largely survive renumbering and relocation.

C1.justification: V1 presents discovery and pricing as coequal innovations and explicitly claims the first effective joint data/model search. V2's title, abstract, and introduction prioritize instrumental-value pricing and frame discovery as an implementation building on existing techniques. Learning the buyer prior becomes an additional central challenge.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning applicability without a known buyer prior, robustness to estimation error, and the learning-speed/stability tradeoff. Appendix A.2 discusses misleading augmentation rankings caused by differing model quality. V1's substantive privacy discussion and market-segmentation rationale are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly documents rechecking top-t augmentations under a common model and reports t = log n as sufficient in experiments. RQ3 and Appendix D.2 supply learning schedules, batch/round settings, and beta-distribution parameters. These are additional technical disclosures; they do not establish reruns of the retained benchmarks.

R1.justification: V2 removes the dedicated Data Valuation/Data Shapley discussion and much privacy-related positioning. It adds instrumental-value references by Ai and colleagues and Castro Fernandez, plus Doob and Schwartz for Bayesian consistency. Discovery is repositioned as a Metam-based implementation supporting the pricing contribution.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and architecture exposition are extensively rewritten. Pricing precedes discovery, whose former standalone treatment is redistributed into evaluation and Appendix A. Pricing-baseline descriptions move to Appendix D.1, and new learning and proof sections substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds nine multi-panel learning figures and removes the separate School/Taxi figure. Existing architecture, Markov-chain, aggregate discovery, and pricing graphics are relocated or resized. Wrapped figures, denser page formatting, and running preprint headers substantially change the presentation.

improvement.justification: The prior learner and sensitivity experiments provide useful progress beyond v1's assumed known buyer prior. However, v2's new revenue-robustness guarantee is not established by Appendix C as written: its transition-error argument ends with a buyer-utility bound without deriving the revenue bound in Definition 5.1. RQ3 measures distributional KL error rather than revenue under learned priors, while the original pricing evidence remains unchanged. The useful extension and unresolved support for its economic guarantee prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
